# 3.2 Example 1

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Back in Chapter 1, we were able to rely entirely upon inference
indicator expressions when recognizing arguments; if a passage contained
an inference indicator expression, then it was an argument, and if a
passage didn't contain an inference indicator expression, then it wasn't
an argument.

Things got a little more complicated in Chapter 2, when we encountered
explanations. Since explanations can contain inference indicator
expressions just like arguments do, we can't just assume that any
passage containing an inference indicator expression is an argument.
Instead, we need to ask ourselves, "What is this passage doing?"
Arguments try to convince us *that* something is true. Explanations try
to account for *why* something is the case.

With this in mind, let's take a look at the following passage. **"What
is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us that something is
true?"**

> "Why do people want to put some criminals to death instead of
> sentencing them to life in prison with no possibility of parole? It's
> because a lust for vengeance is hardwired into our brains as part of
> our evolutionary heritage. Sometimes, only capital punishment will
> satisfy that lust."

The first thing we might notice is the location of the reason indicator
expression "because."

> "Why do people want to put some criminals to death instead of
> sentencing them to life in prison with no possibility of parole? It's
> **because** a lust for vengeance is hardwired into our brains as part
> of our evolutionary heritage. Sometimes, only capital punishment will
> satisfy that lust."

If this were an argument, the claim that a lust for vengeance is
hardwired into our brains—the claim following the "because"—would be
given as a reason for us to believe that people want to put some
criminals to death. But this passage doesn't try to convince us that
people want to put some criminals to death and it doesn't try to
convince us that the death penalty is justified. Instead, this passage
confines itself to explaining *why* people advocate the death penalty, a
fact which we are assumed to know already. Consequently, this passage
contains an explanation, not an argument.

Sometimes, people report that the more arguments they encounter, the
more likely they are to mistake an explanation for an argument. That's
normal. When people are mastering a hammer, everything can start to look
like a nail. The key is to ask yourself, "Is this passage trying to
convince me that something is true?" If not, it isn't an argument.

## Summary of Example 1

This example presented us with the following passage:

> "Why do people want to put some criminals to death instead of
> sentencing them to life in prison with no possibility of parole? It's
> because a lust for vengeance is hardwired into our brains as part of
> our evolutionary heritage. Sometimes, only capital punishment will
> satisfy that lust."

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked ourselves, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to
convince us that something is true?"**

Because this passage is accounting for why something is true without
attempting to convince us that it is true, this passage contains an
explanation, not an argument.
